questions.prompt: What does `fork()` return in the CHILD process?
questions.explain: The child gets 0 and the parent gets the child's pid; -1 means the call failed. That difference is how the two tell themselves apart.

questions.prompt: What does `fork()` return in the PARENT process?
options: The pid of the new child
Nothing: it does not return in the parent
questions.explain: The parent receives the pid of the child it has just created.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (It runs with standard output going to a pipe.)
questions.explain: The child changes ITS copy of `x`. The parent waits, then prints its own copy, which is still 1.

questions.prompt: How many lines does this program print? Type the lines (they are all alike).
questions.explain: Both processes continue after each fork: after two forks there are four processes, and each prints one line.
The parent waits for the child to end before it prints, so the order is fixed.

questions.prompt: How many processes exist (the original one included) after `fork(); fork(); fork();`?
questions.explain: Every fork doubles the number of processes: 2 x 2 x 2 = 8.

questions.prompt: How many processes exist after `for (i = 0; i < 3; i++) fork();`?
questions.explain: The children also run the loop, so every iteration doubles the count: 2^3 = 8.

questions.prompt: A child that has ended but whose parent has not yet called `wait` is called a {{0}}.
questions.explain: The system keeps its pid and exit status until the parent collects them. `ps` shows it as `<defunct>`.

questions.prompt: What does a child get from its parent through `fork`?
options: The same point of execution (it continues after the fork)
questions.explain: The child is a clone: copies of the data, the same open files and the same program counter. Only the pid (and ppid) differ.
option_notes: False: it has a new pid.

questions.prompt: Which call makes a parent wait until one of its children ends?
questions.explain: `wait` blocks until a child ends and returns its pid.

options: The value the child passed to `exit`
The signal that killed the child
1 if the child ended and 0 if it is running
questions.explain: It extracts the exit code (0 to 255) from the status that `wait` stored.

questions.prompt: When is it correct to use `WEXITSTATUS(status)`?
options: Only if the child was killed
questions.explain: A child killed by a signal has no exit code: check `WIFEXITED` first.

questions.prompt: What does this program print when its standard output is a pipe or a file (not a terminal)?
questions.explain: Without a newline the `a` stays in the stdio buffer, and `fork` copies that buffer into the child. Each process then writes `a` in front of its own text: `ab` and `ac`. A `fflush(stdout)` before the fork would print it once.

questions.prompt: Put in order what happens when a parent creates a child and waits for it.
items: The system creates the child as a copy of the parent
The parent's `wait` returns with the child's status
questions.explain: After the fork two processes run concurrently; the parent's `wait` returns only when the child has ended.

questions.prompt: In Linux, what happens to a child whose parent ends first?
options: It is adopted by `init` (or a subreaper) and keeps running
It becomes a zombie that never goes away
questions.explain: Orphans are adopted by process 1, which reaps them when they end. (The slides mention "cascading termination"; that happens on other systems, not on Linux.)

questions.prompt: Match each call with what it does.
pairs: creates a copy of the calling process
waits for a child to end
gives the pid of the parent
replaces the program that is running
questions.explain: These are the basic process calls of the topic.

questions.prompt: `waitpid(pid, &st, WNOHANG)` returns 0. What does that mean?
options: The child has not ended yet
questions.explain: With `WNOHANG` the call does not block: 0 means the child exists but is still running.

options: It returns the pid of the child that ended
It returns -1 when the process has no children to wait for
It lets you choose which child to wait for
It blocks until some child ends
questions.explain: `wait` takes ANY child. To pick one, use `waitpid`.
option_notes: True: that is how a loop `while (wait(&st) > 0)` ends.
